question: On 7 October 2023, Hamas fighters infiltrated Israel and killed more than 1200 people. People who knew what was going to happen treacherously profited from the terrible death toll. Predictably, Israeli share prices have fallen as a result of the escalation of the conflict.

Law professors Robert Jackson Jr of New York University and Joshua Mitts of Columbia University claim in a preliminary report that unknown traders might possibly have known about Hamas's plans to attack Israel so as to make use of the information and, through short selling, profit from falling prices there1.
The Israel Securities Authority announced that it was aware of the matter and that ‘all relevant parties’ were investigating it. 1.
What knowledge does the Commission have about these events?
Is an investigation being conducted in the EU, too, into whether there were incongruities as regards short selling and derivatives transactions in this connection?
What conclusions does the Commission draw from these events?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.3.

2024) Regulation (EU) No 596/2014 on market abuse (‘MAR’)1 establishes a common regulatory framework to prevent market abuse, such as insider dealing or market manipulation and to ensure the integrity of financial markets in the EU, whereas Regulation (EU) No 236/20122 on short selling and certain aspects of credit default swaps (‘SSR’) lays down strict rules on short selling and gives the competent authorities temporary powers to require greater transparency or impose restrictions on short-selling in periods of exceptional financial instability in the whole or in part of the EU.

National Competent Authorities (NCAs) shall ensure that MAR provisions are observed regarding market abuse carried out on their territory, and market abuse carried out abroad relating to instruments traded or admitted to trading on a trading venue operating within their respective territories.

NCAs are also in charge of ensuring that all short sales of financial instruments or derivatives related to financial instruments admitted to trading on a trading venue in the EU, including when they are traded outside the trading venue, comply with the SSR. The alleged incidents reported in the media occurred in the Tel Aviv and United States stock exchanges.

The Commission does not have evidence of similar activity occurring in the EU. However, if NCAs have reason to believe that such activity, as described by the Honourable Member, has occurred in their jurisdictions, they are responsible for investigating the matter and for taking action.

The role of the European Securities and Markets Authority under Regulation (EU) No 1095/20103 is to ensure the consistent and effective application of the MAR and SSR by NCAs, including through the use of supervisory convergence tools.
